script.name: Aortic stenosis

epidemiology.who: Older adults with age-related calcification of a normal valve, and younger adults with a bicuspid valve

script.pathophysiology: The aortic valve calcifies and narrows, obstructing left ventricular outflow. The ventricle hypertrophies concentrically to keep up its output and eventually fails. Coronary flow cannot meet the thick wall's oxygen demand, which causes angina.

timeline.onset: Silent for decades; symptoms appear once the stenosis is severe
timeline.course: Once symptoms start, survival without valve replacement is short

exam: harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids
slow-rising, weak carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus)
soft or absent second heart sound
labs: BNP rises as the ventricle fails
imaging: echocardiogram showing a calcified valve, a small valve area and a high gradient

criteria: Severe aortic stenosis: mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity 4 m/s or more, or a valve area of 1 square centimeter or less

first_line: aortic valve replacement for severe stenosis with symptoms or an ejection fraction below 50%: transcatheter (TAVR) or surgical (SAVR)
TAVR is preferred for older patients and those at high surgical risk
serial echocardiograms while asymptomatic; earlier replacement is increasingly offered for severe disease
next_line: balloon valvuloplasty as a bridge in unstable patients
cautious diuresis; avoid strong vasodilators, which can drop blood pressure

confused_with.how_to_tell_apart: Both cause a systolic ejection murmur, but the murmur of aortic stenosis radiates to the carotids and gets softer with Valsalva, while the murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy gets louder with Valsalva or standing. Aortic stenosis is a disease of older adults; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is inherited and shows up in the young.

Aortic stenosis is a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids; mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.
Aortic stenosis is a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur with a slow-rising pulse; aortic regurgitation is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur with a wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses.

pearls: The murmur of aortic stenosis gets softer with Valsalva and standing, because less blood fills the ventricle.
The classic symptoms of severe aortic stenosis are syncope, angina and dyspnea from heart failure.
Severe aortic stenosis with GI bleeding from angiodysplasia is Heyde syndrome.

sources.title: 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease
2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease
